{"result": "# Reduck

Reduck automates any website through reusable browser scripts, filling the gaps where no official API exists. A script is addressed as `[<handle>/]<host>/<slug>` — discover one with `list_scripts`, read its contract with `read_script`, run it with `run_script`.

## Where scripts run

Every script runs on a **device**: a browser paired to your account through the Reduck extension. The automation inherits that browser's state — the sites you're signed into, its fingerprint — so a script that needs a login usually just works, and credentials never leave your machine. Pair from the extension's side panel; `list_devices` shows what's paired.

You can pair several browsers, each with its own device id. `browser` picks _where_ a run happens: omit it for your paired browser, `"extension"`/`"local"` to auto-pick your single device of that kind, or `{deviceId}` (equivalently the `deviceId` shorthand) to pin one — auto-pick fails if 2+ match. `"managed"` runs on a Reduck managed browser and needs a privileged account; it also takes `region`/`country`. A managed run spends browser time, and `country` additionally spends residential-proxy bandwidth — `whoami` shows both against this period's quotas.

What to run is one object: `script: {host, slug, handle?, args?}` — a script's `args` live with that script, never at the top level of the call. Each `run_script` opens a **fresh** browser.

To run several scripts, pass `scripts` — a list of those same objects, each with its own `args`. They run **at the same time, one browser each**, so this is how to fan out: one call instead of N. They share nothing (no cookies, no DOM, no order) and one failing doesn't stop the others, so you get one outcome per entry in the order you passed them, plus a `batchId`. Each entry takes its own slot on the target's concurrency budget, so more scripts than slots just queue and drain — `queued` means busy, not offline.

A run id and a batch id are different ids, and each answers for exactly one thing: `read_run_results({runId})` always reports that ONE run (its result or error) even when it belongs to a batch, while `read_run_results({batchId})` reports every script in the batch at once. The step trace and its screenshots live behind `read_run_trace({runId})`.

## Owners

Any owner handle scopes `list_scripts` / `read_script` / `run_script`: `reduck` for the curated catalogue, `@user` (with @) for a user's scripts, `project` (without @) for a project's. Omit `handle` for your own.

To iterate on an existing script: `create_draft_script_version` creates a persisted draft; test it with `run_script({script: {version_id}})`, then `promote_script_version` to make it current. Use `list_script_versions` to see all versions (IDs, draft status, notes), and `delete_draft_script_version` to discard a draft you abandoned. To build or modify scripts, load the authoring doc from the index below.

## Available docs

Load with `read_docs({name})`.

- `authoring_scripts` — Build Reduck scripts — discover selectors live via exec_code, crystallize into saved scripts. Load before writing or modifying any script.

# Authoring Reduck scripts

A Reduck script is a Playwright script meant to create an API on top of a website's UI. Each script is one endpoint, and it is 1:1 with the site: one thing the site lets a person do (search, read a page, send a message), with args the site takes and output information the page contains.

A script **MUST NOT** hold business logic. It does not filter, rank, score or decide on what it returns. That belongs in a Skill or in the code that calls the script.

A good script has three properties, in this order:

- **Reliable**: it reaches the right answer on every path the site can take (signed out, another language, a dialog, nothing to show) and in every condition it runs in (beside other runs on one browser, a slow machine, a run window the user minimized). When it cannot, it says what the page showed.
- **Accurate**: it returns what the site holds, all of it, as the site gives it.
- **Fast enough**: it does what the task needs and no more.

## Scope

The contract for every primitive a script and `exec_code` run against: builtins, buildutils, `ai` and the selector grammar. A saved script has the same scope, minus `buildutils`.

Builtins:
goto(url: string, opts?: { waitUntil?: "commit"|"domcontentloaded"|"load"|"networkidle", timeout?: number }) — navigate to url → the main document Response (.status(), .url()), or null. Waits for domcontentloaded by default: wait for the content you need next. An HTTP error status is returned, not thrown.

type(sel: Sel, text: string) — focus and fill (clears first)
paste(sel: Sel, text: string) — paste text via CDP insertText: one shot, fires real input events, drives rich/contenteditable editors. Clears first, like type.
hover(sel: Sel) — hover (reveal hover-only UI)
scrollTo(sel: Sel) — scroll element into view
waitFor(sel: Sel, state="visible", opts?: { timeout?: number }) — wait for selector. state ∈ visible|attached|hidden|detached.

## The form of a script

A script, a library, and the code of `exec_code` and `exec_trace` are modules. The module's default export is called with the scope as one object, and what it returns is the result:

```typescript
export default async ({ page, builtins, args }) => {
	await builtins.goto("https://example.com");
	return { title: await page.title() };
};
```

- A body with a top-level `return` is refused by `exec_code` and `exec_trace` before it runs, and fails to load as a script.

```typescript
import type { Args, Output } from "reduck:contract";
```

## How to write scripts

### Making a mental model of the site with `buildutils`

To fix a script, start from its failing runs and what each page showed. To build one, explore the site first.

Reduck provides first class tooling for this called `buildutils`. You use them while you build, in `exec_code` on a live browser. They work the way a dev looks at a page to create an automation script: you look at a screenshot, point at what you want, and they tell you which element is there and how to select it.

- `screenshot`: see what the page shows now.
- `peek(x, y)`: point at a spot and get the selector of the element under it.
    - `x, y` are page coordinates, not screenshot coordinates: after a scroll, add the scroll offset (`y + scrollY`), or peek finds nothing.
    - Inside a list row, peek often returns the row itself (`getByTestId('tweet')`), not the field you pointed at. Use it to find the row, then `show` to find the fields inside it.
- `show(selector)`: see every element a selector matches. One match is good; zero or several means the selector is wrong.
    - For a list, the count is the check: one match per row means the selector is right.
- `requests`: every request the session's tabs sent since the session started, the first page load included, as Playwright Requests. Use it to find which request carries the data.
- `scroll`: move the page, or one list on it, to bring more into view.
- `clickAt(x, y)` and `wait(n)`: click a spot, or pause. For exploring only.

The loop: look, point, check, act, look again. Use it to find what to click on, how to select it reliably, and where the data you want to read is.

To learn what the app sends, do one action in the UI (a filter, the search box, one scroll), then read with `buildutils.requests()` which request it sent and what changed in it. One action per control is enough: that request is the spec. Scroll with `buildutils.scroll`: a scroll set from page code (`scrollTop`) often loads nothing.

```js
const sent = (await buildutils.requests())
	.slice(before)
	.filter((r) => r.url().includes("/graphql"));
return sent.map((r) => r.url());
```

### Building reliable and reusable scripts with our `builtins` primitives

`builtins` are browser primitives we have curated to perform key browser actions: go to a URL, click, type, paste, hover, press a key, drag, download, upload. They act on the page. **Selectors are first class.** `builtins` take a CSS string or a ReduckSelector: a list of steps (`role`, `test-id`, `nth`, `frame-locator`…) that maps to a Playwright locator. It is the format `peek` returns, so a selector found while exploring goes straight into the script.

Websites have often core code patterns repeated across pages. To match this, each site has a library: code shared across scripts. When the site changes, the fix lands in one file, and every script that imports it moves to the fix at once, when you promote that version.

- The library holds what the site is: how to open it and know it is ready, how to tell a block page or a signed-out page, how to read its recurring shapes.
- The script holds the one affordance it exposes: its args, its URL, its output.

The input, output and description are the API the caller sees. They choose and use the script from these three alone.

So the job is split in two scripts:

1. `suggest_locations` gives the id:

```js
suggest_locations({ query: "Paris" });
// → { locations: [{ label: "Paris, Île-de-France, France", geoUrn: "106383538" }, …] }
```

2. `search_people` takes the id and puts it in the URL. It never types or clicks:

```js
search_people({ keywords: "founder", geoUrn: "106383538" });
```

**A run gets no page from an earlier run.** Outside your own debugging session, a run never sees a page an earlier run left open; only the account's state carries over (the sign-in, a cart). So a script opens what it needs itself, and returns what a later call needs (an id, a URL, a cursor).

**A write that acts on what a read showed checks that it is still true.** The site can change between two runs: a price, an item in the cart, the card.

- The read returns a hash of the data the write acts on: all of it and nothing more. Leave out text that moves with the clock, such as a delivery date written as "tomorrow".

### Patterns for reliable scripts

#### Context: what a run works with

1. **Chrome is built for a person looking at one page.** It does visual work only when someone could see it. A run has nobody looking at it.
2. **A page has three layers.** The network (the answers the site sends), the page's memory (its elements and its code), and the pixels (what Chrome draws). Each layer depends on the one below it.
